analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to disclose their top donors and closes loopholes for foreign money in elections.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 188 House cosponsors, all Democrats, but has sat in three committees with no action and no path to a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require corporations, super PACs, unions, and tax-exempt 'dark money' groups that spend more than $10,000 influencing federal elections to report that spending to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, including who their big donors are. It would tighten the ban on foreign money in elections, make it a crime to set up a shell company to hide foreign election spending, and require political ads to name the top funders behind them. It has not moved since it was referred to three House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn within a day which corporations, unions, and nonprofit groups are paying for the political ads they see, and who those groups' biggest donors are. Candidates who already disclose their donors would face outside spending groups that no longer can hide theirs. Federal agencies would get new tools to trace foreign money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to follow the money

how_it_helps.text: Organizations that spend more than $10,000 on election-related communications must report it to the FEC within 24 hours, identifying their beneficial owners and every donor who gave $10,000 or more.

The bill extends the existing ban on foreign national spending to digital and online ads, to ballot initiative and referendum campaigns, and to communications about federal judicial nominations, and directs the GAO to study illicit foreign money in each four-year election cycle.
It becomes a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to set up or use a corporation or other entity with the intent to conceal a foreign national's election contribution.

Video and online political ads paid for by outside groups must include a statement of who approves the message and a list of the group's top five funders (top two for audio ads), and the same disclosure rules extend to spending for and against federal judicial nominees.

The bill's findings state that dark money groups spent an estimated $1.05 billion in the 2020 election cycle and that current law imposes few transparency requirements on the corporate and nonprofit spending the Supreme Court permitted in Citizens United.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, super PACs, 501(c)(4) 'social welfare' groups, and labor unions that spend on elections would lose the ability to fund campaigns anonymously and would take on new reporting duties. Large online platforms and ad networks would have to carry expanded disclaimers and funder lists. Political operatives who route money through shell entities would face criminal exposure.

drawbacks.text: Once a group crosses the $10,000 spending threshold, it must file reports within 24 hours under penalty of perjury, a compliance burden that falls hardest on small nonprofits and grass-roots organizations without legal staff.

The disclosure rules reach beyond candidate elections to 'issue' communications in election years and to advertising about federal judicial nominations, sweeping in political speech that does not involve voting for a candidate.

Naming a group's top donors can expose them to harassment; the bill includes an exemption for people facing serious threats, but the bill's text specifies that social ostracism, negative commentary, or criticism do not qualify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large: voters would know, in near real time, who is bankrolling the ads trying to sway their votes and their courts. The costs are real but narrower, mainly compliance work for groups that spend on politics and less anonymity for their donors, and the bill includes exceptions for ordinary business dealings and for donors facing genuine threats. On balance, the transparency gains outweigh the administrative burden, though the breadth of what counts as an election communication is a legitimate concern for issue advocates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees, and none of them has taken it up, so it has never come near a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas introduced the bill on March 4, 2026, with 188 original cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
It was referred to the Committees on House Administration, Ways and Means, and Judiciary, and no further action appears in the bill's record.
No Republican cosponsor has joined, and with Republicans controlling all three committees and the House floor calendar, the bill has no scheduled path forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: corporations, super PACs, and tax-exempt groups that spend on elections without disclosing their donors remain unaffected, and their biggest-spending players face no new scrutiny this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 188 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republicans have signed on, and Republican committee chairs control whether the bill ever gets a hearing or a vote.

industries.industry: Dark money nonprofit groups (501(c)(4)s and super PACs)
industries.note: These groups spent an estimated $1.05 billion in the 2020 cycle without naming donors; the bill would force them to disclose big funders within 24 hours of major spending. Their business depends on voters not knowing who is behind the ads, which runs directly against the public's interest in tracing the money.

Companies would have to identify beneficial owners and donors behind campaign spending, ending the anonymity the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision left in place. Ordinary voters are the intended beneficiaries of that transparency.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and ad networks
industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more U.S. users would have to carry expanded disclaimers and top-funder lists on political ads, adding compliance work, but they keep the political ad revenue either way.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill and would owe the same 24-hour disclosures as corporations, a real administrative cost. Union political spending generally backs candidates and causes aligned with their members, so the transparency requirement is a burden they share with, not against, ordinary workers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no Republican cosponsors, and every committee it sits before is chaired by a Republican in a Republican-controlled House. Historically, DISCLOSE Acts have stalled in committee or failed Senate procedural votes requiring 60 senators. Unless leadership changes course, the most likely path is that the bill dies at the end of this Congress without a hearing or a vote.
